rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question does not specify whether it asks what wine and gambling are, whether they may be used, or whether drinking is lawful; the answer about sin implies a question about permissibility.
rows.anchor: ليس فيه بيان أنهم عن أي شيء سألوا ، فإنه يحتمل أنهم سألوا عن حقيقته وماهيته

rows.speaker: عمر ومعاذ ونفر من الصحابة
rows.claim: A report of the staged prohibition says wine was initially lawful, then Umar, Muadh, and other Companions asked for a ruling because it ruins reason and wealth, prompting this verse; some drank and others abstained.
rows.anchor: ثم إن عمر ومعاذا ونفرا من الصحابة قالوا : يا رسول الله أفتنا في الخمر

rows.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن عوف
rows.claim: At a meal hosted by Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, guests drank, became intoxicated, and one recited the opening of al-Kafirun incorrectly; this occasioned the prayer-time restriction.
rows.anchor: ثم دعا عبد الرحمن بن عوف ناسا منهم ، فشربوا وسكروا

rows.speaker: سعد بن أبي وقاص وعمر
rows.claim: After intoxicated Ansar, including Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas, boasted and exchanged insulting verse, an Ansari split Saʿd's head with a camel jaw; Umar prayed for decisive clarification, and the final prohibition followed, to which he assented.
rows.anchor: أنشد سعد شعرا فيه هجاء للأنصار

rows.speaker: القفال
rows.claim: Al-Qaffal explains the staged prohibition as compassionate gradualism: people were accustomed to wine and benefited from it, so an immediate ban would have burdened them.
rows.anchor: والحكمة في وقوع التحريم على هذا الترتيب أن الله تعالى علم أن القوم قد كانوا ألفوا شرب الخمر

rows.speaker: ومن الناس من قال
rows.claim: An alternative chronology says this verse prohibited wine first, the prayer verse then prohibited drinking at prayer time (implicitly stopping drinking since an intoxicated person cannot pray), and al-Maida made the ban emphatic.
rows.anchor: الناس من قال بأن الله حرم الخمر والميسر بهذه الآية

rows.speaker: الربيع بن أنس
rows.claim: Al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas reports that this verse came down after wine had already been prohibited.
rows.anchor: وعن الربيع بن أنس أن هذه الآية نزلت بعد تحريم الخمر

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shafiʿi defines wine broadly: every intoxicating drink is khamr.
rows.anchor: قال الشافعي رحمه الله : كل شرب مسكر فهو خمر

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abu Hanifa defines khamr narrowly as strong grape juice that has thrown up foam.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو حنيفة : الخمر عبارة عن عصير العنب الشديد الذي قذف بالزبد

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn Umar reports that when wine was prohibited, it was made from five substances: grapes, dates, wheat, barley, and maize; Razi uses this to show these drinks were all called wine and covered by the prohibition.
rows.anchor: عن الشعبي عن ابن عمر رضي الله عنهما ، قال : نزل تحريم الخمر يوم نزل وهي من خمسة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi draws three implications from Ibn Umar's report: wine included drinks from all five sources, the prohibition reached all five, and Umar treated every mind-altering drink as wine; Umar's linguistic authority strengthens the last point.
rows.anchor: ولا شك أن عمر كان عالما باللغة ، وروايته أن الخمر اسم لكل ما خامر العقل فغيره

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Al-Nuʿman ibn Bashir transmits the Prophet's statement that wine can come from grapes, dates, honey, wheat, and barley; Razi says this explicitly brings those drinks under the verse.
rows.anchor: روى أبو داود عن النعمان بن بشير رضي الله عنه قال : قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: الخطابي
rows.claim: Al-Khattabi says the five sources are named because they were familiar then, not exclusive; maize, sult, and tree extracts share their rule, as unlisted usury goods share the rule of the six named goods.
rows.anchor: قال الخطابي رحمه الله : وتخصيص الخمر بهذه الأشياء الخمسة ليس لأجل أن الخمر لا يكون إلا من هذه الخمسة

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Ibn Umar transmits the Prophet's statement that every intoxicant is wine and every intoxicant is forbidden.
rows.anchor: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم : ( كل مسكر خمر ، وكل مسكر حرام )

rows.speaker: الخطابي
rows.claim: Al-Khattabi reads the report either as defining the Arabic or a new legal name for all intoxicants, or as declaring them legally equivalent to wine if the literal linguistic claim is impossible.
rows.anchor: قال الخطابي : قوله عليه السلام ( كل مسكر خمر )

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: In response to a question about betʿ, the Prophet says every intoxicating drink is forbidden; betʿ is a honey drink, and the answer gives no allowance for small amounts.
rows.anchor: روى أبو داود عن عائشة رضي الله عنها أنها قالت : سئل رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم عن البتع ، فقال : ( كل شراب أسكر فهو حرام )

rows.speaker: الخطابي
rows.claim: Al-Khattabi argues the betʿ report refutes permissive interpretations of nabidh and the claim that a small quantity of an intoxicant is lawful: the categorical answer covers the whole class and all amounts.
rows.anchor: قال الخطابي : البتع شراب يتخذ من العسل ، وفيه إبطال كل تأويل يذكره أصحاب تحليل الأنبذة

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Jabir reports the Prophet's rule that whatever intoxicates in a large amount is forbidden even in a small amount.
rows.anchor: روى أبو داود عن جابر بن عبد الله ، قال : قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم : ( ما أسكر كثيره فقليله حرام )

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: A report from Aisha says every intoxicant is forbidden and even a handful is unlawful if a farq of the drink intoxicates; al-Khattabi defines a farq as sixteen ratls, showing the ban covers every part.
rows.anchor: روى أيضا عن القاسم عن عائشة ، قالت : سمعت رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يقول : ( كل مسكر حرام

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Umm Salama reports that the Prophet forbade every intoxicant and every drink that causes bodily torpor; al-Khattabi defines mufattir as inducing lassitude and numbness.
rows.anchor: روى أبو داود عن شهر بن حوشب ، عن أم سلمة ، قالت : نهى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم عن كل مسكر ومفتر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi concludes that the hadiths collectively establish that every intoxicant is wine and forbidden.
rows.anchor: فهذه الأحاديث كلها دالة على أن كل مسكر فهو خمر ، وهو حرام

rows.speaker: أهل اللغة
rows.claim: Linguists derive khamr from covering: khimar covers the head, khamr can conceal something, and khamartu means covering a vessel; Razi takes the derivation to support concealment of the intellect.
rows.anchor: قال أهل اللغة : أصل هذا الحرف التغطية ، سمي الخمار خمارا لأنه يغطي رأس المرأة

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbari says khamr is so named because it mixes with the intellect; Razi cites Kathir's verse using the phrase dāʾ mukhāmir as evidence for the sense of intermixture.
rows.anchor: ابن الأنباري : سميت خمرا لأنها تخامر العقل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi links covering and mixing: what mixes with something veils it; intoxication covers reason and blocks its light from reaching the limbs, so the name denotes an intoxicant.
rows.anchor: لأن الشيء إذا خالط الشيء صار بمنزلة الساتر له ، فهذه الاشتقاقات دالة على أن الخمر ما يكون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi rejects the objection that this proves a language by analogy: derivation identifies a word's referent, just as Hanafis derive intercourse for nikah and restraint for fasting.
rows.anchor: لأنا نقول : ليس هذا إثباتا للغة بالقياس ، بل هو تعيين المسمى بواسطة هذه الاشتقاقات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi says the community recognizes three wine-related verses: two use khamr, while the prayer verse refers to intoxication, confirming that khamr means an intoxicant.
rows.anchor: أن الأمة مجمعة على أن الآيات الواردة في الخمر ثلاثة واثنان منها وردا بلفظ الخمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because Umar and Muadh sought a ruling on wine as a destroyer of reason and wealth, Razi argues that anything with the same effect must be wine or share its ruling.
rows.anchor: سبب تحريم الخمر هو أن عمر ومعاذا قالا : يا رسول الله إن الخمر مسلبة للعقل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi reads al-Maida's stated harms—enmity, hatred, and diversion from remembrance and prayer—as certainly caused by intoxication, making intoxication the rationale and prohibition applicable to every intoxicant.
rows.anchor: ولا شك أن هذه الأفعال معللة بالسكر ، وهذا التعليل يقيني ، فعلى هذا تكون هذه الآية نصا

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة وأصحابه
rows.claim: Abu Hanifa's side cites the blessing of making sugar and good provision from palms and grapes, arguing that the drink at issue is among God's blessings and therefore permissible.
rows.anchor: من الله تعالى علينا باتخاذ السكر والرزق الحسن ، وما نحن فيه سكر ورزق حسن

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas reports that at the Farewell Pilgrimage the Prophet declined a household nabidh offered by al-Abbas, then accepted it diluted with Zamzam and said to cut strong drinks with water.
rows.anchor: روى ابن عباس أنه عليه الصلاة والسلام أتى السقاية عام حجة الوداع فاستند إليها ، وقال : اسقوني

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة وأصحابه
rows.claim: The Hanafi argument infers from the Prophet's frown and dilution with water that the drink was strong and that dilution removed its intensity.
rows.anchor: وجه الاستدلال به أن التقطيب لا يكون إلا من الشديد ، ولأن المزج بالماء كان لقطع الشدة بالنص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi answers the blessing argument: an indefinite mention of sugar and good provision does not prove that the disputed nabidh is meant; the earlier verse was superseded or qualified by the later prohibitions.
rows.anchor: نكرة في الإثبات ، فلم قلتم : إن ذلك السكر والرزق الحسن هو هذا النبيذ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi suggests the offered nabidh may have been water with dates that slightly soured it; the Prophet's delicate taste could explain his frown without implying intoxication.
rows.anchor: فلعل ذلك النبيذ كان ماء نبذت تمرات فيه لتذهب الملوحة فتغير طعم الماء قليلا إلى الحموضة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi adds that water may have been poured in to remove sourness or odor, not to reduce intoxicating strength; he judges the opposing inference too weak against his evidence.
rows.anchor: كان المراد بصب الماء فيه إزالة ذلك القذر من الحموضة أو الرائحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since Companion reports conflict, Razi says they should be set aside in favor of the apparent wording of the Qur'an and the Prophet's Sunna.
rows.anchor: وأما آثار الصحابة فهي متدافعة متعارضة ، فوجب تركها والرجوع إلى ظاهر كتاب الله وسنة الرسول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi argues that wine contains sin, and sin is forbidden by al-Aʿraf 7:33; together the verses prove wine prohibited.
rows.anchor: والإثم حرام لقوله تعالى : { قل إنما حرم ربي الفواحش ما ظهر منها وما بطن والإثم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whether ithm means punishment or the sins that deserve punishment, it can only describe what is forbidden; calling the sin greater than the benefit likewise entails prohibition.
rows.anchor: وقد يراد به ما يستحق به العقاب من الذنوب

rows.speaker: منهم من قال
rows.claim: Some deny that the verse prohibits wine: it says wine contains sin rather than that drinking is sinful, so the sin could be incidental rather than a ban on drinking.
rows.anchor: الآية لا تدل على أن شرب الخمر إثم ، بل تدل على أن فيه إثما

rows.speaker: منهم من قال
rows.claim: Some argue that the verse cannot prohibit wine because it explicitly recognizes benefits in it, and prohibited things cannot be beneficial.
rows.anchor: أنه تعالى أثبت فيها منافع للناس ، والمحرم لا يكون فيه منفعة

rows.speaker: منهم من قال
rows.claim: Some object that if this verse already prohibited wine, the later prayer restriction and al-Maida prohibition would have been unnecessary.
rows.anchor: لو دلت هذه الآية على حرمتها فلم لم يقنعوا بها حتى نزلت آية المائدة وآية تحريم الصلاة

rows.speaker: منهم من قال
rows.claim: Some argue that if the great sin applied whenever wine existed, its prohibition would have had to hold in every religious community.
rows.anchor: فلو كان ذلك الإثم الكبير سببا لحرمتها لوجب القول بثبوت حرمتها في سائر الشرائع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi answers that the question concerns wine generally, so its sin necessarily accompanies it under every circumstance; drinking entails that forbidden consequence and is itself forbidden.
rows.anchor: فلما بين تعالى أن فيه إثما ، كان المراد أن ذلك الإثم لازم له على جميع التقديرات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi answers that immediate worldly benefit does not prevent something from being forbidden; a specific benefit does not negate the general ruling.
rows.anchor: أن حصول النفع العاجل فيه في الدنيا لا يمنع كونه محرما

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Razi cites Ibn Abbas as reporting that the verse was revealed to prohibit wine; no report says the Companions hesitated, and senior Companions could seek a stronger statement as Abraham sought reassurance about resurrection.
rows.anchor: أنا روينا عن ابن عباس أنها نزلت في تحريم الخمر ، والتوقف الذي ذكرته غير مروى عنهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi answers the appeal to earlier communities by reading the statement as describing the present condition: wine harmed this community then, though it had not harmed earlier peoples.
rows.anchor: أن قوله : { فيهما إثم كبير } إخبار عن الحال لا عن الماضي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maysir means gambling and is the verbal noun of yasara, as mawʿid and marjiʿ derive from their verbs; yassartuhu means I gambled it.
rows.anchor: الميسر القمار ، مصدر من يسر كالموعد والمرجع من فعلهما ، يقال يسرته إذا قمرته

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil derives maysir from ease, since it takes another's wealth effortlessly, or from yasar, affluence, because gambling can make one wealthy.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل : اشتقاقه من اليسر لأنه أخذ لمال الرجل بيسر وسهولة من غير كد ولا تعب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says that in pre-Islamic times a man would wager his family and property.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس : كان الرجل في الجاهلية يخاطر على أهله وماله

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba derives maysir from apportioning: the camel is named for being divided, the butcher for portioning it, and gamblers are called yasirun because they divide its meat.
rows.anchor: ابن قتيبة : الميسر من التجزئة والاقتسام

rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi derives maysir from yassara li, meaning that something became due; the lot-winner is the one made entitled by the arrows.
rows.anchor: قال الواحدي : إنه من قولهم : يسر لي هذا الشيء ييسر يسرا وميسرا إذا وجب

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshaf describes ten named arrows used to divide a slaughtered camel into ten shares (or twenty-eight, excluding three blank arrows); each arrow had a fixed allotment.
rows.anchor: قال صاحب ( الكشاف ) : كانت لهم عشرة قداح ، وهي الأزلام والأقلام

rows.speaker: شاعر لم يسمه المصدر
rows.claim: An unnamed poet lists waghad, safih, and manih as arrows with no winnings, illustrating the arrow names in the gambling practice.
rows.anchor: لي في الدنيا سهام … ليس فيهن ربيح وأساميهن وغد … وسفيح ومنيح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The arrows were shaken in a bag by a trusted person, then drawn for each player; winners took their marked meat shares, while blank-arrow players received nothing and paid for the whole camel.
rows.anchor: يجعلونها في الربابة ، وهي الخريطة ويضعونها على يد عدل ، ثم يجلجلها ويدخل يده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The players gave the meat to the poor rather than eating it themselves, took pride in doing so, and disparaged nonparticipants as baram.
rows.anchor: وكانوا يدفعون تلك الأنصباء إلى الفقراء ، ولا يأكلون منها ، ويفتخرون بذلك ويذمون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi reports disagreement over whether maysir names the camel-arrow game alone or all gambling.
rows.anchor: اختلفوا في أن الميسر هل هو اسم لذلك القمار المعين

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A Prophetic report warns against two dice as a form of Persian gambling.
rows.anchor: عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: ابن سيرين ومجاهد وعطاء
rows.claim: Ibn Sirin, Mujahid, and Ata regard any game involving a stake as gambling, even children's play with nuts.
rows.anchor: عن ابن سيرين ومجاهد وعطاء

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: Ali classifies backgammon and chess as gambling.
rows.anchor: عن علي عليه السلام أنه قال

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shafiʿi permits chess when there is no wager, obscene speech, or neglect of prayer; without a transfer of money it is neither gambling nor maysir.
rows.anchor: وقال الشافعي رضي الله عنه

rows.speaker: أهل الاتفاق
rows.claim: The scholars agree that wagers in races involving hoofed animals or horses are not maysir; the detailed rules are treated in the jurisprudence chapter on racing and archery.
rows.anchor: في الخف والحافر فبالاتفاق ليس من الميسر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reason is humanity's noblest faculty and restrains base impulses like a camel's tether; wine removes that restraint, so drinking is among the vilest acts.
rows.anchor: أن عقل الإنسان أشرف صفاته ، والخمر عدو العقل ، وكل ما كان عدو الأشرف فهو أخس

rows.speaker: ابن أبي الدنيا
rows.claim: Ibn Abi al-Dunya recounts seeing a drunk man urinate into his hand as if performing ablution, praising Islam as light and water as pure.
rows.anchor: ذكر ابن أبي الدنيا أنه مر على سكران وهو يبول في يده ويمسح به وجهه

rows.speaker: العباس بن مرداس
rows.claim: Al-Abbas ibn Mirdas explains that he refused wine despite claims it increased courage: he would not swallow his ignorance or be a leader by morning and a fool by night.
rows.anchor: وعن العباس بن مرداس أنه قيل له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi cites al-Maida's account of wine causing enmity and hatred and diverting people from remembrance and prayer as further harms.
rows.anchor: ما ذكره الله تعالى من إيقاع العداوة والبغضاء والصد عن ذكر الله وعن الصلاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike other sins, repeated drinking strengthens desire and activity; it immerses a person in bodily pleasure and heedlessness of the afterlife, until God makes them forget themselves.
rows.anchor: فإنه كلما كان إقدامه عليه أكثر ، كان نشاطه أكثر ، ورغبته فيه أتم

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Razi cites the Prophetic saying that wine is the mother of evils, since loss of reason opens the way to every vice.
rows.anchor: ولذلك قال عليه الصلاة والسلام : ( الخمر أم الخبائث )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gambling's sin lies in the enmity caused by insults and disputes, taking another's property unjustly, and distracting people from remembrance and prayer.
rows.anchor: وأما الميسر فالإثم فيه أنه يفضي إلى العداوة ، وأيضا لما يجري بينهم من الشتم والمنازعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wine brought merchants profit because imported wine sold at high prices, and buyers who did not haggle were considered generous and honorable.
rows.anchor: منافع الخمر أنهم كانوا يتغالون بها إذا جلبوها من النواحي ، وكان المشتري إذا ترك المماكسة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People attributed many bodily and emotional benefits to wine: strength, digestion, sexual vigor, consolation, courage, generosity, complexion, warmth, and ambition.
rows.anchor: ومنها أنه يقوي الضعيف ويهضم الطعام ويعين على الباه ، ويسلي المحزون ، ويشجع الجبان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gambling could transfer meat to needy people; al-Waqidi says a player might win a hundred camels in one gathering and distribute the proceeds, earning praise.
rows.anchor: وذكر الواقدي أن الواحد منهم كان ربما قمر في المجلس الواحد مائة بعير

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: Hamza and al-Kisaʾi read kathīr, many, arguing that wine and gambling bring numerous sins, the Prophet cursed ten connected to wine, and harms contrast with many benefits.
rows.anchor: قرأ حمزة والكسائي { كثير } بالثاء المنقوطة من فوق والباقون

rows.speaker: باقي القراء
rows.claim: The other readers say kabīr, great; Razi favors this reading because sin is magnified by greatness, supported by Quranic usage, and all readers use kabīr in the comparative phrase that follows.
rows.anchor: حجة الباقين أن المبالغة في تعظيم الذنب إنما تكون بالكبر لا بكونه كثيرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The spending question had already been answered by identifying the recipient; it is repeated here to answer how much to give. Observing the call to generosity, people asked whether they must give everything or only part, and God accepts al-ʿafw.
rows.anchor: اعلم أن هذا السؤال قد تقدم ذكره فأجيب عنه بذكر المصرف وأعيد ههنا فأجيب عنه بذكر الكمية

rows.speaker: القفال
rows.claim: Al-Qaffal compares this answer to describing a person's beliefs and character when asked what they are like: the response gives relevant qualities rather than a literal definition.
rows.anchor: قال القفال : قد يقول الرجل لآخر يسأله عن مذهب رجل وخلقه ما فلان هذا
